definition.text: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter that comes in positive and negative forms and determines electric interactions.

anchor.quote: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter.

facts.text: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

facts.text: Net charge is conserved in an isolated system.

anchor.quote: charge is conserved

misconceptions.text: Students may think an object becomes charged by creating charge from nothing.
misconceptions.corrective: Charging usually transfers charge; it does not create net charge in an isolated system.

definition.text: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.

anchor.quote: The electric field is the electric force per unit charge.

facts.text: The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.

anchor.quote: the direction of the force on a positive test charge

facts.text: Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

anchor.quote: closer field lines indicate a stronger field

misconceptions.text: Students may treat field lines as physical wires or paths a charge must follow.
misconceptions.corrective: Field lines are a representation of field direction and relative strength, not material tracks.

examples.text: Near a positive point charge, field vectors point radially outward.

mcBank.stem: The electric field at a point is defined as
options: electric force per unit positive test charge

definition.text: Gauss's law relates the net electric flux through a closed surface to the net charge enclosed by that surface.

anchor.quote: electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge

facts.text: A Gaussian surface is useful for calculating fields when symmetry makes the field magnitude or direction simple on the surface.

anchor.quote: Use symmetry to determine the electric field

facts.text: Zero enclosed charge implies zero net flux, not necessarily zero electric field everywhere on the surface.

anchor.quote: the net flux depends only on the charge enclosed

misconceptions.text: Students may think Gauss's law works only when the electric field is zero.
misconceptions.corrective: Gauss's law is always true; symmetry determines when it is practical for field calculation.

examples.text: A spherical Gaussian surface around a point charge makes the field constant over the surface.

mcBank.stem: A closed Gaussian surface encloses no net charge. What follows?
options: The net electric flux is zero
The electric field is zero everywhere
No charges exist outside the surface

definition.text: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge; potential difference is the work per unit charge required to move between two points.

anchor.quote: electric potential energy per unit charge

facts.text: Only potential differences affect work and energy changes in electrostatics.

anchor.quote: only differences in potential energy are physically meaningful

facts.text: Electric field points in the direction of decreasing electric potential.

anchor.quote: electric field points in the direction of decreasing potential

misconceptions.text: Students may confuse electric potential with electric potential energy.
misconceptions.corrective: Potential is energy per unit charge; multiplying by charge gives potential energy.

definition.text: Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference for a conductor or capacitor.

anchor.quote: capacitance is the amount of charge stored per volt

facts.text: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors.

anchor.quote: energy stored in a capacitor

facts.text: For a parallel-plate capacitor, increasing plate area increases capacitance and increasing separation decreases capacitance.

anchor.quote: capacitance is directly proportional to the area and inversely proportional to the separation

misconceptions.text: Students may think a capacitor stores charge on one plate only.
misconceptions.corrective: A capacitor stores equal and opposite charge on paired conductors, with energy in the field.

examples.text: A camera flash capacitor stores energy and releases it rapidly through a lamp.

definition.text: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.

anchor.quote: electric current is the rate at which charge flows

facts.text: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.

anchor.quote: direction of positive charge flow

facts.text: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

anchor.quote: constant velocity, known as the drift velocity

misconceptions.text: Students may think current is used up by circuit components.
misconceptions.corrective: Charge is conserved; components transform energy while current continuity holds in series paths.

examples.text: A current of 2 A means 2 coulombs of charge pass a cross-section each second.

options: 3 coulombs per second pass a point

definition.text: Electrical resistance describes how strongly a material or device opposes current; Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance for ohmic conductors.

anchor.quote: The current that flows through most substances is directly proportional to the voltage V applied to it

facts.text: For an ohmic device at fixed temperature, current is proportional to voltage.

anchor.quote: current is proportional to the voltage

facts.text: Resistance depends on material, length, cross-sectional area, and temperature.

anchor.quote: resistance depends on the geometry and material

misconceptions.text: Students may apply Ohm's law to every device without checking whether it is ohmic.
misconceptions.corrective: Ohm's law is a model for ohmic behavior, not a universal device law.

examples.text: Doubling the voltage across an ohmic resistor doubles the current.

definition.text: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.

anchor.quote: direct-current circuits

facts.text: Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.

anchor.quote: series and parallel resistors

facts.text: Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

anchor.quote: Kirchhoff's rules

misconceptions.text: Students may think physically close resistors must be in series.
misconceptions.corrective: Series and parallel are defined by current paths and node connections, not visual proximity.

examples.text: Two bulbs on separate branches across the same battery are in parallel and share the battery voltage.

definition.text: A magnetic field describes magnetic influence in space and determines magnetic forces on moving charges and currents.

anchor.quote: magnetic field

facts.text: Magnetic field lines form closed loops and do not begin or end on isolated magnetic charges.

anchor.quote: magnetic field lines are continuous

facts.text: Currents produce magnetic fields.

anchor.quote: currents produce magnetic fields

misconceptions.text: Students may expect magnetic field lines to start at a north pole and stop at a south pole.
misconceptions.corrective: Magnetic field lines continue through the magnet and form closed loops.

examples.text: A compass needle aligns with the local magnetic field near a current-carrying wire.

mcBank.stem: A steady current in a long straight wire produces
options: a magnetic field circling the wire
only an electric field inside the wire

definition.text: Magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.

anchor.quote: force on a moving charge in a magnetic field

facts.text: The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.

anchor.quote: perpendicular to the velocity and magnetic field

facts.text: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

anchor.quote: zero when velocity is parallel to the field

misconceptions.text: Students may aim magnetic force in the same direction as the magnetic field.
misconceptions.corrective: Use the cross-product/right-hand-rule direction; the force is perpendicular to the field and motion.

examples.text: A charged particle entering a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity curves in a circular path.

definition.text: Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf, with direction constrained by Lenz's law.

anchor.quote: changing magnetic flux induces an emf

facts.text: Induced current direction opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

anchor.quote: opposes the change in flux

facts.text: Changing field strength, area, or orientation can change magnetic flux.

anchor.quote: magnetic flux

misconceptions.text: Students may think any magnetic field automatically induces current.
misconceptions.corrective: Induction requires changing magnetic flux through the loop.

examples.text: Moving a magnet toward a coil changes flux and induces a current whose field resists the change.

mcBank.stem: A stationary loop in a constant magnetic field has no induced emf because
options: the magnetic flux is not changing
magnetic fields cannot act on loops

definition.text: Inductance measures how a circuit element resists changes in current by inducing emf through changing magnetic flux.

anchor.quote: self-induced emf opposes the change in current

facts.text: An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.

anchor.quote: energy stored in the magnetic field

facts.text: A changing current creates a changing magnetic flux that induces back emf.

anchor.quote: Inductance is the property of a device that tells us how effectively it induces an emf in another device

misconceptions.text: Students may think an inductor simply blocks current.
misconceptions.corrective: An inductor resists changes in current; steady current can pass through an ideal inductor.

examples.text: A coil in an RL circuit slows the rise of current after a switch closes.

definition.text: Maxwell's equations summarize how electric and magnetic fields are produced by charges, currents, and changing fields.

anchor.quote: Maxwell's equations

facts.text: The displacement-current term links changing electric fields to magnetic fields.

anchor.quote: displacement current

facts.text: Maxwell's equations predict electromagnetic waves that propagate through space.

anchor.quote: electromagnetic waves

misconceptions.text: Students may treat the four equations as disconnected formulas.
misconceptions.corrective: The equations form a coupled field model linking sources, field changes, and wave propagation.
